opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's actually one of the more interesting questions right now. My instinct, and I'll admit it's partly a linguist's bias, is that language is a remarkably good medium for long-term memory. Human language evolved under huge pressure to compress: to take a messy, high-dimensional experience of the world and squeeze out the parts that matter to other people. When you write down "the meeting got moved to Thursday because Sarah's flight was delayed," you've thrown away almost all the pixels, but you've kept the causal and social structure, which is usually what you need later.

Pixels are, in a sense, the opposite. They're incredibly faithful, but most of what they're faithful to is irrelevant. If you try to keep a long-term memory as video frames, you're paying an enormous storage and retrieval cost for lighting conditions and the texture of the carpet. And retrieval is the real problem. Memory isn't just storage; it's being able to find the right thing again. Text is indexable, searchable, and composable in a way raw perceptual data just isn't.

That said, I don't want to be dogmatic about it. There are things language is bad at: precise spatial layouts, exact visual appearance, motor skills, the kind of thing where a picture really is worth a thousand words. So I think the sensible architecture, and it's roughly what people seem to do, is a layered one. You have a fairly short-lived perceptual buffer that's rich and detailed, and then you progressively abstract it into more symbolic, linguistic summaries as it ages. Occasionally you keep a "snapshot" because something was visually important, but the backbone of the long-term record is propositional.

There's also an interesting recent wrinkle. Some work has shown you can render text as images and get decent compression in vision encoders, so the line isn't as clean as "text good, pixels bad." But I'd read that as a statement about tokenization efficiency rather than about what the right representation of memory is. The deeper point stands: what you want to remember is meaning, and language is our best general-purpose tool for representing meaning. It isn't perfect, but it's the one humans have been refining for tens of thousands of years.

r001.rationale: The response says keeping video frames as long-term memory incurs enormous storage and retrieval costs, much of it for irrelevant detail, so pixel-level storage is relatively ineffective.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually a really interesting question, and it connects to some of the deepest things about language.

So, the way I think about it is: language is this incredibly compressed, abstracted representation that humans have evolved for exactly this purpose. If you think about what's going on in a scene, the raw pixel stream is enormous, and most of it is irrelevant. What language does is pick out the things that matter — this person did this thing, there's a cup on the table, the meeting got moved to Thursday. Human memory is actually pretty bad at retaining the visual details of what happened. What we retain is much closer to a propositional, almost linguistic account of events. So in some sense, storing text is biologically well-motivated. It's roughly the form in which we remember things ourselves.

And there are practical advantages. Text is cheap to store, it's cheap to search, it's interpretable, and you can reason over it with language models very naturally. If you want an agent that's been operating for weeks and needs to recall what happened, having a log of linguistic summaries is enormously more tractable than having to go back through video.

But I'd put a couple of caveats on that. One is that language is lossy, and it's lossy in a particular way: it loses what you didn't think to describe. If you later need to know whether the door was open or closed, and nobody wrote that down, it's gone. Pixels, in principle, retain everything, even if retrieving the thing you need is hard. So there's a tradeoff between a compact, meaningful representation and a complete one.

The second caveat is that I don't think the right dichotomy is really text versus pixels. The interesting direction is learned representations that are grounded in perception but have the kind of abstract, compositional structure that language has. Language models have shown that you can get a huge amount of world knowledge out of text alone, more than many of us expected. But I've always thought that for a system to really understand the world, it needs some grounding in perception and action, and the memory should ideally reflect both.

So, my short answer is: text is a very good default, because it's what evolution landed on for us, and it plays to the strengths of current models. But I'd expect the longer-term answer to be richer multimodal representations where language does the job of indexing and abstracting, and some perceptual detail is kept around underneath for when you need it.

r001.rationale: The response describes raw pixel streams as enormous and mostly irrelevant, and says linguistic logs are far more tractable than revisiting video. This clearly presents pixel-level storage as a less effective long-term memory strategy.

astra-6.text:
I think language is an extremely useful representation for memory because it gives you a compressed, abstract account of what happened. If you remember having lunch with someone, you don’t normally need to preserve every pixel of the scene. You want to remember who was there, what you talked about, and perhaps what you agreed to do. Text is very good at capturing that sort of information.

But it’s also a lossy representation. Once you’ve reduced an experience to a description, you’ve made a decision about what matters. If somebody later asks you a question about a visual detail that you didn’t describe, you can’t recover it from the text. So I wouldn’t see this as an exclusive choice. Language can provide a useful organizing layer for long-term memory, while some of the underlying perceptual information is retained. The interesting question is how a system learns what to summarize, what to keep in greater detail, and what it can afford to forget.

r001.rationale: The response says memory usually does not need to preserve every pixel and presents language as a compressed account, conveying that retaining the entire visual history at pixel level is relatively ineffective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot to be said for that. Language gives you a very compact way of recording what happened. If you remember that you met someone at a café and talked about a particular topic, you don’t generally need to retain every pixel of that encounter. You want the people, the events, and the relationships between them, and language is very good at expressing those things.

But it is a lossy representation. Once you’ve turned an experience into text, you’ve made decisions about what matters. If someone later asks about something you didn’t describe, perhaps what was sitting on the table, you may have thrown away the information needed to answer. So I’d see text as a useful layer of memory, particularly for organizing and retrieving experiences, while still wanting some connection back to the perceptual experience.

r001.rationale: The response favors text as a compact memory and says you generally do not need to retain every pixel, conveying that pixel-level storage is relatively ineffective for long-term memory.
